title: Dictionaries & Sets
description: Organize data by key and work with unique unordered collections

lessons.title: Dictionaries Basics
lessons.description: Store key-value pairs for fast lookups

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create dicts, access/add/update values by key, and check for a key's presence.

sections.title: 🗂️ Creating & Accessing
sections.content:
A dictionary maps unique keys to values.

```python
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
person["name"]        # 'Alice'
person.get("email")   # None (no error if missing)
person.get("email", "n/a")  # 'n/a' (default)
```

sections.title: ✏️ Adding & Updating
sections.content:
```python
person["email"] = "a@example.com"  # add new key
person["age"] = 31                  # update existing key
del person["age"]                    # remove a key
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using `person["missing_key"]` and getting a KeyError — use `.get()` when a key might not exist.

questions.question: How do you create an empty dictionary?
questions.explanation: Curly braces (with no key:value pairs) create an empty dict.

questions.question: What happens if you access a missing key with `d[key]`?
questions.explanation: Direct indexing raises KeyError for missing keys.

questions.question: What does `d.get("x", "default")` do?
questions.explanation: get() safely returns a fallback instead of raising.

questions.question: How do you remove a key from a dict?
questions.explanation: del is the standard way, though pop(key) also works.

questions.question: Are dictionary keys required to be unique?
options: Only string keys must be unique
questions.explanation: Assigning to an existing key overwrites its value.

questions.question: What does `person["age"] = 31` do if 'age' already exists?
questions.explanation: Assignment overwrites the existing value for that key.

questions.question: Dictionaries map...
questions.explanation: That mapping is the core concept of a dict.

questions.question: What type of value can a dict key be?
questions.explanation: Keys must be hashable — lists can't be keys, but strings, numbers and tuples can.

lessons.title: Dictionary Methods & Iteration
lessons.description: Loop through dictionaries and use handy methods

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Iterate keys, values, and items; use common dict methods.

sections.title: 🔁 Iterating a Dictionary
🧰 Useful Methods
sections.content:
```python
person.keys()      # dict_keys(['name', 'age'])
person.values()    # dict_values(['Alice', 30])
person.items()     # dict_items([('name','Alice'), ('age',30)])
"name" in person   # True (checks keys)
person.update({"city": "NYC"})  # merge in new pairs
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using `"Alice" in person` expecting to search values — `in` checks keys by default, not values.

questions.question: What does `for key in person:` iterate over?
questions.explanation: Direct iteration over a dict yields its keys.

questions.question: What does `.items()` return?
questions.explanation: items() gives you both parts of each pair for unpacking.

questions.question: What does `"Alice" in person` check?
options: Whether 'Alice' is a KEY in person
questions.explanation: The `in` operator on a dict checks membership among keys.

questions.question: What does `person.update({"city":"NYC"})` do?
options: Adds/overwrites keys from the given dict
Only adds new keys, never overwrites
questions.explanation: update() merges another dict's pairs into this one.

questions.question: How do you loop over both keys and values together?
questions.explanation: items() unpacks neatly into key, value pairs.

questions.question: What does `.values()` return?
questions.explanation: values() gives just the value side of each pair.

questions.question: What is `.keys()` useful for?
options: Getting all key names, e.g. to check membership
questions.explanation: keys() exposes the dict's key set.

questions.question: If you want to check if a value (not key) exists in a dict, you should...
questions.explanation: You must explicitly search .values() to check for a value.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create sets, add/remove elements, and use them to dedupe data.

sections.title: 🎯 Creating Sets
sections.content:
A set holds unique items with no guaranteed order.

```python
nums = {1, 2, 3, 2, 1}
print(nums)   # {1, 2, 3} — duplicates removed automatically!

empty_set = set()   # NOT {} — that's an empty dict!
```

sections.title: ✏️ Modifying Sets
sections.content:
```python
nums.add(4)        # add one item
nums.remove(1)     # remove (errors if missing)
nums.discard(99)   # remove if present, no error otherwise
3 in nums          # membership test, very fast
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing `{}` expecting an empty set — that actually creates an empty dictionary. Use `set()` instead.

questions.question: What does `{1, 2, 2, 3}` become as a set?
questions.explanation: Sets automatically remove duplicate values.

questions.question: How do you create an empty set?
questions.explanation: {} creates an empty dict, not a set — set() is required.

questions.question: What does `nums.discard(99)` do if 99 isn't in nums?
questions.explanation: discard() is the safe version of remove().

questions.question: What does `nums.remove(1)` do if 1 isn't present?
questions.explanation: remove() is strict and errors on a missing element.

questions.question: Are sets ordered?
questions.explanation: Sets don't guarantee any particular order.

questions.question: Why are sets useful for deduplication?
options: They only store unique elements by design
questions.explanation: Converting a list to a set removes duplicates.

questions.question: How do you check membership in a set?
questions.explanation: The in operator works on sets, and is very efficient.

questions.question: What does `nums.add(4)` do?
questions.explanation: add() inserts an element; if it's already there, nothing changes.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference.

sections.title: 🔗 Combining Sets
🧪 Comparing Sets
sections.content:
```python
{1, 2}.issubset({1, 2, 3})    # True
{1, 2, 3}.issuperset({1, 2})  # True
{1, 2}.isdisjoint({3, 4})     # True (no overlap)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting `-` is not symmetric: `a - b` (in a but not b) differs from `b - a` (in b but not a).

questions.question: What does `{1,2,3} | {2,3,4}` return?
questions.explanation: | is the union of both sets.

questions.question: What does `{1,2,3} & {2,3,4}` return?
questions.explanation: & returns only elements in both sets.

questions.question: What does `{1,2,3} - {2,3,4}` return?
questions.explanation: Difference: elements in the first set but not the second.

questions.question: What does `^` compute?
questions.explanation: ^ gives elements unique to each set, excluding overlap.

questions.question: What does `.issubset()` check?
options: If all elements of one set are in another
questions.explanation: issubset checks full containment.

questions.question: `{1,2}.isdisjoint({3,4})` returns...
questions.explanation: Disjoint means no overlap at all.

questions.question: Is `a - b` the same as `b - a`?
questions.explanation: Order matters for set difference.

questions.question: Which operator gives elements common to two sets?
questions.explanation: & is intersection.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Data Structure
lessons.description: Decide between list, tuple, dict, and set

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Pick the right container based on order, mutability, and uniqueness needs.

sections.title: 🧭 Quick Decision Guide
sections.content:
**List** — ordered, mutable, duplicates allowed
→ Use for: sequences you'll modify, e.g. a to-do list.

**Tuple** — ordered, immutable, duplicates allowed
→ Use for: fixed groups of values, e.g. coordinates.

**Dict** — unordered*, mutable, unique keys
→ Use for: labeled data / lookups by key. (*insertion order preserved since Python 3.7)

**Set** — unordered, mutable, unique values
→ Use for: membership tests and removing duplicates.

sections.title: 📊 Side-by-Side Example
sections.content:
```python
# Same data, different structures
as_list  = ["red", "green", "blue"]
as_tuple = ("red", "green", "blue")
as_set   = {"red", "green", "blue"}
as_dict  = {"primary": "red", "secondary": "green"}
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Defaulting to lists for everything — using a set for fast membership checks or a dict for lookups is often much clearer and faster.

questions.question: Which structure guarantees unique elements?
questions.explanation: Sets enforce uniqueness automatically.

questions.question: Which structure is immutable?
questions.explanation: Tuples cannot be changed after creation.

questions.question: Best structure for labeled lookups (e.g. name -> age)?
questions.explanation: Dicts map keys to values directly.

questions.question: Which is fastest for checking 'is x in this collection'?
questions.explanation: Sets use hashing for near-instant membership checks.

questions.question: Which structure would you use for GPS coordinates (fixed pair)?
questions.explanation: Immutable fixed-size data suits a tuple well.

questions.question: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries...
questions.explanation: Modern Python dicts remember the order items were added.

questions.question: Which structure would best model a shopping cart where order and duplicates matter?
questions.explanation: Lists preserve order and allow duplicate entries.

questions.question: Why avoid always defaulting to lists?
options: Other structures can be clearer/faster for their use case
questions.explanation: Choosing the right tool improves both clarity and performance.

exercise.title: Choose the Right Structure
exercise.prompt:
Create four variables using the most appropriate data structure.

1. Shopping items

Order matters and duplicates are allowed:

milk, bread, milk

Create:

shopping_items

2. GPS location

The values should not change:

25.2854, 51.5310

Create:

location

3. User profile

The data has labels:

name → Ali
age → 25
city → Doha

Create:

user_profile

4. Unique programming languages

Duplicates should automatically disappear:

Python, Java, Python, C++

Create:

languages
exercise.starterCode:
# Use a list
shopping_items = []

# Use a tuple
location = ()

# Use a dictionary
user_profile = {}

# Use a set
languages = set()
exercise.hint: List for ordered items with duplicates, tuple for fixed coordinates, dictionary for labeled fields, set for unique values.
